lessons.title: Cold Chain Management and Logistics
lessons.body: In Africa's heat, many medicines like vaccines, insulin, and some antibiotics must stay between 2Â°C and 8Â°C. A break in the cold chain can make them useless or dangerous. You need a reliable refrigerator, a thermometer, and a way to keep things cold during transport. In cities, use a vaccine fridge with a temperature logger. In rural areas, a solar direct-drive (SDD) fridge is best because it doesn't need batteries or fuel. For transport, use a cold box with ice packs. Pre-condition ice packs in a freezer at -20Â°C for at least 24 hours. A standard 5-litre cold box can hold 2 litres of vaccines and stay cold for 24-48 hours if packed correctly: line the sides with ice packs, put vaccines in the middle, and fill empty spaces with bubble wrap. Always put a thermometer inside the box. If the temperature goes above 8Â°C, mark the vaccines as 'do not use' and call your supervisor. Never freeze vaccines that shouldn't be frozen (like DPT or hepatitis B). Freezing can ruin them. Keep a temperature log: record the temperature twice a day, morning and evening. If you see a reading outside 2-8Â°C, act immediately. For longer trips, use a refrigerated truck or a 4x4 with a 12V car fridge. In remote areas, plan your route to avoid midday heat. Use a 'shake test' for freeze-sensitive vaccines: if you suspect freezing, shake the vial and compare to a non-frozen vial. If it's cloudy, discard it. Train your staff on cold chain basics every 6 months. Remember: a broken cold chain wastes money and can kill patients. Simple tools and discipline keep medicines safe.

lessons.title: Wholesale Distribution and Inventory Control
lessons.body: Wholesale distribution means buying medicines in bulk from manufacturers or importers and selling them to pharmacies, clinics, and hospitals. To succeed, you need to control inventory carefully. Start with a simple system: use a stock card or a free app like 'Stock Management' on your phone. Record every item in and out. Set a reorder level for each product. For example, if you sell 100 paracetamol tablets per week, and it takes 2 weeks to get new stock, your reorder level is 200 tablets plus a safety stock of 50. So when stock hits 250, you order more. Use the FIFO method: first in, first out. Always put new stock behind old stock on the shelf. Check expiry dates every month. Remove anything expiring in 3 months and sell it at a discount or return it. Keep a 'fast movers' list: antimalarials, antibiotics, painkillers, and ORS. These should never run out. Slow movers like rare vaccines can be ordered on demand. For storage, keep medicines off the floor on pallets, away from sunlight, and in a dry room below 30Â°C. Use a hygrometer to check humidity; keep it under 60%. Do a physical count every 3 months. Compare with your records. If there's a difference, investigate. Theft and expiry are your biggest losses. Train staff to check expiry dates when receiving goods. For distribution, use a simple route plan: deliver to nearby clinics on Mondays, far ones on Wednesdays. Keep a delivery log with signatures. If you use a motorcycle, use a lockable box. Never leave medicines in a hot car. A good wholesale business runs on accurate records and fast turnover.

lessons.title: Track and Trace Systems and Serialization
lessons.body: Track and trace means following a medicine from the factory to the patient. Serialization gives each pack a unique number, like a fingerprint. In Africa, many countries are adopting GS1 standards. A GS1 DataMatrix barcode is a small square code that holds the product code, batch number, expiry date, and a serial number. You can scan it with a smartphone app like 'GS1 Barcode Scanner' or a handheld scanner. Why does this matter? It stops counterfeiters and helps recalls. If a batch is bad, you can find exactly where it went. To start, ask your supplier for serialized products. When you receive a box, scan the barcode. Your system should record the serial numbers. When you sell to a pharmacy, scan again. This creates a chain. In Kenya, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board uses a system called 'PPB Track and Trace'. In Nigeria, NAFDAC has a similar scheme. For a small business, you don't need a big system. Use a spreadsheet: columns for product name, batch, serial numbers, date received, date sold, and buyer. Keep it on a computer or phone. For high-value items like antiretrovirals, scan every unit. For low-value items, scan the outer box. If you find a product without a serial number, treat it as suspicious. Report it to your national drug authority. Train your staff to scan and verify. A simple rule: no scan, no sale. This protects your reputation and your customers. In the future, blockchain and mobile apps will make this easier, but today, a disciplined paper or spreadsheet system is enough.

lessons.title: Counterfeit Drug Prevention
lessons.body: Counterfeit drugs are fake medicines that may contain no active ingredient, wrong ingredients, or even poison. In Africa, the WHO estimates 1 in 10 medical products is substandard or falsified. You can protect yourself and your customers. First, buy only from licensed suppliers. Ask for a certificate of analysis and a wholesale license. Check the packaging: misspellings, poor printing, and wrong fonts are red flags. Compare with a known genuine sample. Look at the batch number and expiry dateâthey should be printed clearly, not stamped over. Use a simple test: for tablets, check if they dissolve in water within 30 minutes. For syrups, check the smell and colour. But these are not foolproof. Better tools: a 'GPHF Minilab' is a small kit that tests for common drugs like paracetamol, artemether, and antibiotics. It costs about $500 and can be used in a pharmacy. You can also use a 'TruScan' handheld device that uses light to check if the medicine is genuine. In Nigeria, NAFDAC has a 'Green Page' to verify products. In Kenya, use the PPB's online portal. Train your staff to check every delivery. If you suspect a fake, quarantine it, document everything, and report to the national authority. Never sell it. Warn your customers: if a drug doesn't work, it might be fake. Encourage them to buy from you, not from street vendors. Keep a list of known counterfeit products from your regulator. Remember: your reputation is your business. One fake drug can destroy it.

lessons.title: Global Sourcing and Procurement
lessons.body: Global sourcing means buying medicines from manufacturers in other countries. This can save money, but it comes with risks. Start by identifying reliable suppliers. Use platforms like 'Dun & Bradstreet' to check a company's credit and history. Or ask other pharmacists in your network. For essential medicines, the WHO prequalification list is a good starting point. It lists manufacturers whose products meet quality standards. You can also buy from UNICEF's Supply Division or the Global Fund's wambo.org. When you find a supplier, request a proforma invoice. It should include: product name, strength, batch number, expiry date, quantity, unit price, and Incoterms (like FOB or CIF). Incoterms define who pays for shipping and insurance. For small orders, use air freight; for large orders, sea freight is cheaper but slower. Always use a letter of credit (LC) for large payments. An LC is a bank guarantee that you pay only when the goods are shipped. For small orders, use a wire transfer but only after checking references. Watch out for hidden costs: customs duties, clearing fees, and storage at the port. In Africa, clearing can take weeks. Hire a customs agent. Keep all documents: bill of lading, packing list, certificate of analysis, and import permit. In Kenya, you need a permit from the Pharmacy and Poisons Board. In Nigeria, from NAFDAC. Never import without a license. Also, consider local sourcing firstâit's faster and supports your economy. But for specialized drugs, global sourcing is necessary. Build relationships with 2-3 suppliers to avoid shortages. Always inspect goods on arrival. If something is wrong, document it and claim insurance.

lessons.title: Reverse Logistics and Returns
lessons.body: Reverse logistics is the process of moving goods back from the customer to the seller or manufacturer. In pharmaceuticals, returns happen for many reasons: expired stock, damaged goods, wrong items, or recalls. A good returns system protects your money and your reputation. Start with a clear policy: no returns without a receipt and original packaging. For expired goods, many suppliers offer credit notes if you return them before the expiry date. For example, if you return 6 months before expiry, you might get 80% credit; 3 months before, 50%; after expiry, nothing. So track expiry dates monthly. Use a 'returns log' with columns: date, product, batch, quantity, reason, and action. For damaged goods, take photos and file a claim with your supplier or insurer. For recalls, act immediately: contact all customers who bought the batch, quarantine remaining stock, and return to the supplier. In Africa, national regulators like NAFDAC or PPB issue recall notices. You must comply. For unsold goods that are still good, you can donate to clinics or NGOs, but get a receipt for tax purposes. For disposal of expired drugs, never throw them in the bin or flush them. Use a licensed waste disposal company. They incinerate at high temperature. In Kenya, the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) licenses such companies. For small quantities, you can use a 'drug destruction kit' that neutralizes the drug. Keep records of disposal for 5 years. Reverse logistics also includes returning reusable cold boxes and ice packs. Train your staff to handle returns quickly. A smooth returns process builds trust with suppliers and customers.

quiz.q: What is the correct temperature range for most vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Most vaccines must be kept between 2Â°C and 8Â°C to remain effective.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that a vaccine may have been frozen and should not be used?
options: A) It is cloudy after shaking
D) It has a new label
quiz.explanation: Freeze-sensitive vaccines become cloudy after freezing, indicating damage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a temperature log in cold chain management?
options: B) To track temperature twice daily
quiz.explanation: A temperature log helps detect breaks in the cold chain by recording readings twice a day.

quiz.q: Which method is best for keeping vaccines cold during transport in rural areas?
options: B) A cold box with ice packs
D) A refrigerator on a truck
quiz.explanation: A cold box with conditioned ice packs maintains 2-8Â°C for 24-48 hours.

quiz.q: What is the FIFO method in inventory control?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means older stock is sold first to reduce expiry losses.

quiz.q: What is a reorder level?
options: A) The maximum stock you can hold
B) The stock level that triggers a new order
C) The price of the product
D) The number of staff needed
quiz.explanation: Reorder level is the quantity at which you place a new order to avoid stockouts.

quiz.q: Why should medicines be stored on pallets?
options: A) To make them look nice
B) To protect from moisture and pests
quiz.explanation: Pallets keep medicines off the floor, protecting from moisture and pests.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of a counterfeit drug?
quiz.explanation: Misspellings and poor printing are red flags for counterfeit drugs.

quiz.q: Which tool can test for common drugs like paracetamol in a pharmacy?
quiz.explanation: The GPHF Minilab is a portable kit for testing common drugs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect a counterfeit drug?
options: A) Sell it at a discount
C) Return it to the customer
quiz.explanation: Quarantine and report to the national drug authority to protect others.

quiz.q: What is serialization in track and trace?
options: A) Giving each pack a unique number
quiz.explanation: Serialization assigns a unique serial number to each pack for tracking.

quiz.q: Which barcode standard is commonly used for pharmaceuticals?
quiz.explanation: GS1 DataMatrix holds product code, batch, expiry, and serial number.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of track and trace systems?
quiz.explanation: Track and trace allows rapid identification and recall of bad batches.

quiz.q: In Kenya, which body regulates track and trace for medicines?
quiz.explanation: The Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB) regulates medicines in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to start track and trace in a small business?
quiz.explanation: A spreadsheet with columns for serial numbers is a low-cost start.

quiz.q: What is an Incoterm?
options: B) A trade term defining shipping responsibilities
quiz.explanation: Incoterms like FOB or CIF define who pays for shipping and insurance.

quiz.q: Why is a letter of credit used in global sourcing?
options: A) To guarantee payment when goods are shipped
quiz.explanation: A letter of credit ensures payment only after shipment, protecting the buyer.

quiz.q: What document is required to import medicines in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC regulates medicine imports in Nigeria.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when sourcing globally?
quiz.explanation: The WHO prequalification list identifies quality-assured manufacturers.

quiz.q: What is reverse logistics?
options: A) Moving goods from customer back to seller
quiz.explanation: Reverse logistics handles returns, recalls, and expired stock.

quiz.q: What should you do with expired medicines?
quiz.explanation: Expired drugs must be incinerated by a licensed waste company.

quiz.q: What is a common reason for returns in pharmaceuticals?
quiz.explanation: Expired stock is a major reason for returns, often for credit.

quiz.q: What is a credit note?
options: A) A document giving money back or offsetting future purchases
quiz.explanation: A credit note is issued by a supplier for returned goods, reducing amount owed.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of drug disposal for 5 years?
options: A) For tax and regulatory compliance
quiz.explanation: Regulations often require keeping disposal records for several years.

quiz.q: What is a shake test used for?
options: A) To check if a vaccine was frozen
quiz.explanation: The shake test detects freeze damage in vaccines by comparing cloudiness.

quiz.q: What is a solar direct-drive fridge?
options: A) A fridge that runs on solar power without batteries
B) A fridge that uses kerosene
C) A fridge that needs a generator
D) A fridge that uses ice
quiz.explanation: SDD fridges use solar panels directly to cool, no batteries needed.

quiz.q: What is a safety stock?
options: A) Extra inventory to cover unexpected demand
quiz.explanation: Safety stock is a buffer to prevent stockouts during delays.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fast-moving pharmaceutical product?
quiz.explanation: Antimalarials are in high demand and should never run out.

quiz.q: What is the role of a customs agent in global sourcing?
options: A) To clear goods through customs
quiz.explanation: A customs agent handles import paperwork and clearance at the port.

quiz.q: What is a proforma invoice?
options: A) A preliminary bill from supplier before shipment
quiz.explanation: A proforma invoice details goods and costs before a formal order.
